options: 2 true null

questions.q: When may the garbage collector free an object?
questions.explain: Reachability from the roots decides. Other references (from other objects, closures, timers, listeners) keep it alive even after the creating function returns or one variable is cleared.
options: When you set one variable that points to it to null
When the function that created it returns
When it can no longer be reached from any root by following references
When its reference count drops to one

questions.q: Which of these is not a garbage-collection root?
questions.explain: Roots are the starting points: globals, module variables, the stack, and whatever the host holds for you (timers, listeners, pending promise handlers). An object reachable only from garbage is garbage too.
options: A variable declared at the top level of a module
The callback of a pending setInterval
A listener registered on a long-lived event emitter (through the emitter)
An object that is only referenced by another unreachable object

questions.q: An order references its customer and the customer references the order. Nothing else references either. What happens?
questions.explain: Mark-and-sweep starts from the roots, so a cycle that no root reaches is never marked. Only pure reference counting (which JavaScript engines do not rely on) had trouble with cycles.
options: They leak forever, because each keeps the other alive
Both can be collected: neither is reachable from a root
Only the order is collected
JavaScript throws a RangeError for circular references

questions.q: In a garbage-collected language like JavaScript, what is a memory leak?
questions.explain: The collector frees everything unreachable. A leak means you are still holding a path to objects you do not need, so the collector must keep them.
options: Memory the collector forgot to free because of a bug in the engine
Objects the program no longer needs that are still reachable, usually through a reference someone forgot
Any object larger than 1 MB
Memory used by closures

questions.q: Why does V8 split the heap into a young and an old generation?
questions.explain: Temporary objects from each request die quickly and are cleaned up cheaply. A leak shows as an old generation that keeps growing with objects that should have been temporary.
options: Young objects are faster to create
Most objects die young, so collecting a small young area often is cheap; survivors move to the old generation, collected less often
Old objects cannot be collected
To keep strings separate from numbers

questions.q: A module-level Map stores each request's result under the request id "in case it is asked again". Why is this a leak?
questions.explain: A collection with no rule for shrinking grows with traffic until the process runs out of memory. Every growing collection needs a size limit, an expiry, or removal when its owner ends.
options: Maps cannot hold objects
Request ids are unique, so entries are never reused or removed; the module variable keeps every result reachable forever
Maps are cleared by the garbage collector every minute
It is not a leak because the data is in a Map

questions.q: Modules are always in strict mode. What does this print?
questions.explain: In old non-strict scripts, assigning to an undeclared variable silently created a global that lived forever. In strict mode (every module), it throws a ReferenceError instead.
options: ReferenceError
created a global
TypeError
undefined

questions.q: Each request calls priceFeed.addEventListener("change", onChange) on a feed that lives as long as the server, and never removes it. What leaks?
questions.explain: The emitter holds a reference to each listener; each closure holds its request's data. The leak costs memory and CPU time on every event.
options: Nothing; listeners are removed when the request ends
Only the event name
Every listener closure and everything it uses, and every price change now runs all of them
Only the last listener

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first event runs both listeners. Aborting the signal removes every listener registered with it, so the second event runs none.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: removeEventListener needs the very same function object. The second arrow is a new function that was never added, so nothing is removed. Keep a reference to the listener, or use the signal option.
options: TypeError

questions.q: Node prints MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 change listeners added. What should you do first?
questions.explain: The warning fires when one event gets more than 10 listeners, which usually means listeners are added per request or per connection and never removed. Raise the limit only when many listeners are genuinely intended.
options: Call setMaxListeners(0) to silence it
Find out why listeners are added without being removed: it is almost always a real leak
Restart the server
Nothing, it is only a warning

questions.q: A connection starts setInterval(() => ping(session), 30_000) and nobody calls clearInterval when the connection closes. What stays alive?
questions.explain: A pending timer is a root: the host holds its callback until it fires, and an interval fires forever. Clear it in the code that ends its owner's life.
options: Nothing, intervals stop when the connection is closed
Only the interval id
The interval's callback and its closure, including session, forever, and the callback keeps running
The session until the next garbage collection

questions.q: What does timer.unref() do in Node.js?
questions.explain: unref is for background housekeeping timers that should not keep a process alive. It does not free anything and is not a fix for a timer leak.
options: Clears the timer
Makes the timer's callback garbage
Lets the process exit even while this timer is still pending; the timer still fires if the process keeps running
Removes the reference from the closure to its variables

questions.q: Inside loadReport, a large rows array is used by a small debugDump closure that is never called. The function returns a different closure that only uses total. Why can the returned closure keep rows alive?
questions.explain: V8 keeps only variables some closure uses, but it keeps them in one shared context per scope. Any long-lived closure from that scope keeps the whole context, including rows.
options: All closures copy every variable of their scope
Closures created in the same scope share one context object, and rows is in it because debugDump uses it
Arrays are never garbage collected
It cannot; only variables used by the returned closure are kept

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Reading rice moved it to the end (most recently used). When beans made the cache too big, the first key, oil, was the least recently used and was evicted.
options: [ 'rice', 'beans' ]
[ 'oil', 'beans' ]
[ 'rice', 'oil', 'beans' ]
[ 'beans', 'rice' ]

questions.q: What does every production cache need so it cannot leak?
questions.explain: A cache grows by design, so it needs a rule for shrinking. Size limits bound memory; expiry bounds staleness and removes entries nobody reads.
options: A WeakRef around every value
A bound: a maximum size (for example LRU eviction), an expiry time (TTL), or both
To be stored in a global variable
To be cleared on every request

questions.q: You want to cache a computed total for each order object, for exactly as long as the order object exists. Which structure fits?
questions.explain: A WeakMap entry does not keep its key alive, and disappears when the key is collected. A Map would keep every order alive forever.
options: A Map keyed by the order object
A WeakMap keyed by the order object
An array of [order, total] pairs
A WeakRef to the total

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: WeakMap keys are compared by identity. The copy { ...order } is a different object, so it is a cache miss.

questions.q: What must code always handle when it calls ref.deref() on a WeakRef?
questions.explain: A WeakRef does not keep its target alive, so the target can disappear at any time after the current task. Treat undefined as a cache miss and rebuild.
options: A thrown error if the object was collected
A return value of undefined, because the target may have been collected
A promise
Nothing, deref always returns the object

questions.q: Which is a correct use of FinalizationRegistry?
questions.explain: The specification does not promise when, or even whether, a finalization callback runs. Use it only for memory bookkeeping; essential clean-up must be explicit (close(), try/finally).
options: Saving an order to the database when the order object is collected
Closing a file handle reliably
Removing a stale entry from a cache of WeakRefs after its target was collected
Releasing a lock at the end of a request

questions.q: Which process.memoryUsage() field is closest to what a container's memory limit (and an OOM kill) looks at?
questions.explain: rss (resident set size) is all the memory the process holds: heap, code, stacks and buffers. heapUsed is the best number for spotting a JavaScript object leak, but the limit applies to the whole process.
options: heapUsed
heapTotal
rss
arrayBuffers

questions.q: A graph of heapUsed shows a sawtooth: it rises, drops sharply, rises again. The low points stay at the same level over a day. What does it show?
questions.explain: Rising and dropping is normal allocation and collection. A leak shows as a baseline (the low points after each collection) that keeps rising.
options: A memory leak
A healthy process: garbage builds up and is collected, and the baseline is flat
The garbage collector is broken
The process is about to crash

questions.q: This runs in Node.js with forced garbage collection. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both loops allocate the same amount, but after a collection only the kept rows remain. Measuring after garbage collection shows retained memory, not allocation.
options: true true
false true
true false
false false

questions.q: What does a heap snapshot give you that process.memoryUsage() does not?
questions.explain: memoryUsage tells you that memory grows; a snapshot tells you what is on the heap and why it is still reachable.
options: The CPU time of each function
Every live object, its type and size, and the chain of references (retainers) that keeps it alive
A list of all network requests
Nothing more; it is the same number in a file

questions.q: What is the most effective way to find a leak with heap snapshots?
questions.explain: Comparing snapshots isolates what the batch of work left behind. The retainer chain of one leaked object points at the root holding it, and so at the line to fix.
options: Take one snapshot right after startup
Take a snapshot, run a batch of requests, take another, and compare which object types grew; then follow the retainers of a leaked object
Take a snapshot every second in production
Search the snapshot for the word "leak"

questions.q: Why should you not casually take heap snapshots on a busy production server?
questions.explain: Use staging, or take one instance out of the load balancer first. Node can also write a snapshot automatically near the heap limit with --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit.
options: Snapshots delete objects
Writing one pauses the process and needs roughly as much extra memory as the heap itself
Snapshots are only allowed in browsers
They reset the garbage collector

questions.q: A team's fix for a leak is "restart the service every night". What is wrong with that?
questions.explain: A leak grows with work done, not with time. More traffic means a crash sooner. Reproduce it, snapshot, compare, and fix the reference.
options: Nothing; it is the standard fix
It hides the leak until traffic grows enough to crash between restarts, and drops users' connections every night
Restarts make the leak worse
Node.js cannot be restarted

questions.q: Finish createLru(max): get marks a key as most recently used, and set evicts the least recently used key when there are more than max entries.
questions.explain: A Map keeps insertion order, so deleting and re-inserting a key moves it to the end. The first key is then always the least recently used, and is the one to evict.

questions.q: Finish openTracker() so that both listeners are registered with one AbortController's signal, and close() removes them.
questions.explain: The signal option ties every listener to one controller. Aborting it removes all of them, without keeping references to the listener functions.

questions.q: Finish memoizeByObject(fn) using a WeakMap, so each object's result is computed once and does not keep the object alive.
questions.explain: The WeakMap holds each result only as long as its key object is reachable elsewhere, so the memo cannot grow beyond the objects the program is still using.

questions.q: The connection's close() does not stop its heartbeat, so it keeps running. Store the interval and clear it in close().
questions.explain: A pending interval is a root that keeps its callback and closure (here session) alive and running. The code that ends the connection's life must clear it. (leftovers only exists so the starter can end.)

questions.q: The recent map keeps every request forever. Change remember so the map never holds more than 3 entries, dropping the oldest first.
questions.explain: A Map iterates in insertion order, so its first key is the oldest. Deleting it whenever the size passes the limit bounds the memory, however much traffic arrives.

questions.explain: A listener added with { once: true } is removed right after it runs for the first time, so it cannot pile up. It still stays registered if the event never fires, which is where the signal option helps.

questions.q: stopWatching tries to remove the listener with a new arrow function, which removes nothing. Keep a reference to the listener in startWatching and remove that same function.
questions.explain: removeEventListener matches by function identity. Two arrow functions with the same code are two different functions, so you must keep and pass the one you added.

questions.q: Finish createTtlCache(ttlMs, now): get returns undefined and deletes the entry when it is older than ttlMs. The clock is injected as now, so the test does not wait.
questions.explain: Store the time each entry was written. On read, an entry older than the TTL is treated as missing and deleted, so stale data is neither returned nor kept.
